42913766.label: Objective
42913766.text: Lung cancer screening (LCS) with low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) reduces lung cancer-specific and all-cause mortality, yet uptake remains low. This study evaluates LungCheck, a theory-informed multicomponent behavior change and implementation strategy designed to increase LDCT ordering in two diverse primary care settings.

42913766.label: Methods
42913766.text: This pilot study compared 16-month pilot and pre-pilot periods at a federally qualified health center (FQHC) and an academic faculty practice in New York City. LungCheck comprised educational meetings, materials and clinician reminders, an implementation blueprint, patient navigation, and EHR modifications. LDCT ordering rates (primary outcome) were compared using generalized estimating equations (GEE). Post-implementation surveys assessed acceptability, appropriateness, and feasibility.

42913766.label: Results
42913766.text: A total of 5,918 patient-period observations were included (1,569 academic; 4,349 FQHC). Among patients with documented LCS eligibility, the odds of LDCT ordering were significantly higher during the pilot at both the academic practice (OR, 2.67; 95% CI, 1.47-4.85; p=0.001) and FQHC (OR, 4.53; 95% CI, 2.29-8.94; p<0.001). A combined-site multivariable model adjusting for site, age, sex, and race confirmed higher odds of LDCT ordering during the pilot (OR, 1.95; 95% CI, 1.44-2.63; p<0.001). Among patients with an LDCT order, completion was 71.4% (10/14) pre-pilot versus 35.7% (15/42) during the pilot at the academic practice and 42.9% (18/42; 95% CI, 28%-59%) versus 39.3% (24/61; 95% CI, 27%-53%) at the FQHC. The strategy was rated as highly acceptable (AIM, 4.47/5), appropriate (IAM, 4.44/5), and feasible (FIM, 4.41/5).

42913766.label: Discussion
42913766.text: LungCheck was associated with significantly increased LDCT ordering at both sites, high acceptability, feasibility, and appropriateness ratings and high provider knowledge, confidence, and perceived skills related to LCS. Although a corresponding improvement in LDCT completion was not observed, the small number of LDCT orders limited the precision of completion estimates. Persistent environmental and patient-level barriers underscore the need to adapt LungCheck into a multilevel intervention addressing patient-, provider, and system-level barriers across the LCS continuum, to be evaluated in a future cluster randomized trial.

42926166.text: Somatostatin receptor (SSTR) PET has become a central imaging tool in neuroendocrine tumors (NETs), with established roles in detection, staging, restaging, and selection of patients for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy (PRRT). Despite its high sensitivity and target specificity, interpretation is not always straightforward. Physiological SSTR expression, focal variants of normal biodistribution, technical and administration-related artifacts, inflammatory conditions, and benign or malignant non-neuroendocrine lesions may all generate uptake that mimics NET involvement. Conversely, small lesion size, partial-volume effects, high physiological background, and genuinely low or absent receptor expression may reduce lesion conspicuity and lead to false-negative or underestimated disease. Interpretive challenges have also become more relevant as SSTR PET is increasingly used for quantitative, longitudinal, and theranostic assessment. Somatostatin analogue treatment can modify normal-organ biodistribution and lesion-to-background contrast, while liver and spleen uptake may vary substantially across serial examinations and should not necessarily be considered stable reference tissues. In addition, inter-lesional differences in receptor expression may have practical implications when SSTR PET is used to assess suitability for PRRT, because intense uptake in part of the disease does not necessarily imply adequate target expression across all clinically relevant lesions. This review summarizes the principal physiological variants and false-positive and false-negative findings encountered on SSTR PET and discusses contemporary pitfalls related to biodistribution, receptor heterogeneity, quantitative interpretation, and theranostic decision-making. Accurate interpretation requires integration of molecular, anatomical, and clinical information rather than reliance on isolated uptake intensity or a binary positive/negative classification.

42966716.text: The year 2025 brought long-term outcome data supporting coronary CT angiography (CCTA)-guided management of stable chest pain, a proposed reframing of coronary artery disease around atherosclerosis rather than ischemia, and the first large-scale real-world evaluation of a national artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled CT-derived fractional flow reserve (FFR-CT) program. This review summarizes selected advances in cardiovascular computed tomography (CCT) published in print or online during 2025. The studies span coronary artery disease outcomes and prevention, quantitative plaque analysis, photon-counting detector CT, coronary artery calcium scoring, pericoronary inflammation imaging, AI and machine learning, structural and congenital heart disease, and consensus and training documents. For each study we summarize the design, principal findings, limitations, and likely clinical implications, and we close with the barriers, including technical standardization, vendor-specific thresholds, equitable access, and the need for randomized outcome trials, that must be addressed before many of these advances can be implemented broadly.

42986516.label: Objectives
42986516.text: Precise lesion localisation on prostate MRI-specifically, identification of whether at the apex, mid-gland, or base-is essential for effective communication and clinical management. This study aimed to assess interobserver agreement of current practice using the Prostate Imaging-Reporting and Data System (PI-RADS) against a novel anatomy-based approach, P-SMART (Prostate Simplified MRI Anatomy Recognition and Training).

42986516.label: Materials and methods
42986516.text: This multi-reader, two-phase agreement study, used axial and sagittal T2-weighted MRI from a publicly available dataset. Forty MRI cases were annotated with four regions of interest (ROIs). Readers were asked to document ROI location-apex, mid-gland, or base-first using the PI-RADS method, then following a 3-week washout period and short educational intervention, using the P-SMART method. Interobserver agreement was evaluated using Fleiss' kappa (κ) statistics and compared following bootstrap resampling using a paired t-test. Subgroup analyses were performed by reader expertise and prostate size.

42986516.label: Results
42986516.text: Following quality assurance, 156 ROIs were evaluated by 43 readers in each phase of the study. Overall interobserver agreement improved with P-SMART vs PI-RADS (κ = 0.571 vs 0.399; p < 0.001). In subgroup analyses, improvements were consistent for experts (0.663 vs 0.435; p < 0.001), non-experts (0.530 vs 0.393; p < 0.001), large prostates (0.518 vs 0.325; p < 0.001), and small prostates (0.620 vs 0.461; p < 0.001).

42986516.label: Conclusion
42986516.text: The P-SMART approach, designed to align with the PI-RADS sector map, yielded significantly higher interobserver agreement for prostate lesion-level localisation than the PI-RADS method, across reader experience and gland size, though overall agreement was only moderate. Improved reproducibility may support biopsy targeting, active surveillance monitoring, and treatment planning.

42986516.label: Key points
42986516.text: Question Can a novel method of dividing the prostate into apex, mid-gland, and base improve reader agreement compared to current practice? Findings The P-SMART method to divide the prostate outperformed PI-RADS (Fleiss' kappa 0.571 vs 0.399), improving consistency across experience levels and prostate sizes.

42986516.label: Relevance statement
42986516.text: More reproducible prostate level assignment supports accurate lesion localisation for biopsy planning, active surveillance, and treatment planning. If validated, P-SMART may improve communication and could be integrated into reporting workflows and software tools.

42988566.text: C-X-C chemokine receptor type 4 (CXCR4) inhibition may represent a new therapeutic strategy for patients with acute leukemia (AL), not only by increasing chemosensitivity but also by preventing relapse through disruption of residual leukemic cell interactions with the bone marrow niche. Radiolabeled CXCR4 ligands are available for PET imaging ([68Ga]Ga-pentixafor) and radiopharmaceutical therapy (RPT) ([177Lu]Lu-pentixather/[90Y]Y-pentixather). Early clinical experience with CXCR4-targeted RPT, together with the reported feasibility of CXCR4-targeted PET in acute myeloid leukemia, supports the development of theranostic approaches targeting the CXCR4/C-X-C motif chemokine ligand 12-defined leukemia-initiating cell niche. The objective of this study is to determine the maximum tolerated dose (MTD) of a single infusion of [177Lu]Lu-pentixather in patients with relapsed/refractory AL (including both acute myeloid leukemia and acute lymphoblastic leukemia). Methods: PENTILULA is an investigator-initiated, first-in-human, prospective phase 1/2 study based on a standard 3 + 3 dose-escalation design with 5 levels and 3-6 patients per level. Key inclusion criteria include patients with relapsed/refractory AL with CXCR4-positive leukemic cells. The primary endpoint is the incidence and evaluation of dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs) and determination of the MTD. DLTs will be assessed 4-6 wk after RPT and include grade 3 or higher nonhematologic toxicity, prolonged grade 4 pancytopenia with hypocellular bone marrow, and excessive renal or hepatic radiation absorbed dose. The MTD is defined as the highest level at which fewer than one third of patients experience a DLT. In a subset of patients, [68Ga]Ga-pentixafor PET/MRI will be performed to explore the predictive value of theranostic PET imaging on CXCR4 expression, dosimetry, and treatment response. Conclusion: This first-in-human clinical study is ongoing, having reached the fifth and final activity level. [177Lu]Lu-pentixather is being used to definitively establish the MTD and preliminary efficacy of this CXCR4-targeted approach in this high-risk population with limited therapeutic options.

43002566.text: A 76-year-old woman underwent myocardial perfusion Single Photon Emission Computed Tomography (SPECT) using a high-sensitivity cadmium-zinc-telluride camera after administration of 8 mCi 99mTc Methoxyisobutylisonitrile (MIBI). An unexpected diffuse peripheral count distribution was observed. No specific contamination event was identified, and surveys of the detector surface and patient table remained at background levels. Persistent counts on source-free blank imaging despite decontamination initially suggested a possible technical issue. However, serial blank acquisitions demonstrated progressive count reduction consistent with 99mTc physical decay, supporting low-level residual 99mTc contamination. This case demonstrates that high-sensitivity cadmium-zinc-telluride systems may detect low-level contamination not identified by conventional survey measurements.

43020616.text: Prostate-specific membrane antigen (PSMA) PET is an accurate prognostic imaging biomarker of survival in patients with prostate cancer when assessed using Prostate Cancer Molecular Imaging Standardized Evaluation (PROMISE) criteria. Previously, PSMA PET PROMISE risk nomograms were created that surpassed clinical prediction tools. In this study, we focused on the evaluation of quantifiable biomarkers to simplify and facilitate overall survival (OS) prediction. Methods: Data from patients with histologically proven prostate cancer who underwent PSMA PET between December 2012 and April 2024 at participating imaging centers worldwide and who were included in the PROMISE PET Registry by January 31, 2026, were analyzed. Prostate-specific antigen (PSA) levels at PSMA PET, disease stage, and OS follow-up data were collected. PSMA total tumor volume (PSMA TTV) and whole-body SUVmean were assessed using predefined SUV thresholds. PSMA total lesion uptake (PSMA TL) was calculated as PSMA TTV × SUVmean PSA level at PSMA PET adjusted for PSMA TTV was calculated as PSA × TTV. Univariate regression analysis was conducted to identify potential predictors. Prognostic accuracy of quantitative biomarkers was compared using Harrell C-indices and time-dependent concordance in the development cohort. Probabilities for 3-, 5-, and 7-y OS across PSMA TTV quartiles were derived from Kaplan-Meier curves. Subgroup analysis was conducted by cancer stage. Results: In total, 13,893 patients were included in the analysis and divided 2:1 into development (n = 9271) and validation (n = 4622) cohorts. The prognostic accuracy of PSMA TTV in the validation cohort (C-index, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.77-0.80) was superior to SUVmean (C-index, 0.62; 95% CI, 0.61-0.64) and PSA level at PET (C-index, 0.71; 95% CI, 0.69-0.72) and similar to PSMA TL (C-index, 0.78; 95% CI, 0.76-0.79) and PSA × TTV (C-index, 0.77; 95% CI, 0.75-0.78). In the entire cohort, the median OS for PSMA TTV quartile 1 (0 mL) and quartile 2 (>0-2.1 mL) was not reached. The median OS was 11.4 y (interquartile range, 10.1 y to not reached) for PSMA TTV quartile 3 (>2.1-16.2 mL) and 4.4 y (interquartile range, 4.2-4.6 y) for quartile 4 (>16.17 mL). Conclusion: Among quantifiable PET metrics, PSMA TTV had the highest prognostic accuracy for OS in patients with prostate cancer. Automated PSMA TTV assessment may facilitate fast and reproducible outcome prediction in the future.

43062466.label: Objective
43062466.text: To evaluate the robust visualization of photon-counting CT (PCCT) for right adrenal vein (RAV) across body mass index (BMI) groups with respect to virtual monochromatic imaging (VMI) energy levels and reconstruction kernels.

43062466.label: Methods
43062466.text: A total of 302 patients who underwent contrast-enhanced abdominal PCCT were enrolled and stratified into non-obese, overweight, and obese groups based on Asian-specific BMI criteria. VMIs were reconstructed at 40, 55, and 70 keV with three vascular‑specific reconstruction kernels (Bv40, Bv48, Bv60). For quantitative evaluation, two radiologists assessed image metrics, including CT attenuation, image noise (standard deviation [SD]), signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), and contrast-to-noise ratio (CNR). Separately, another pair of radiologists independently evaluated qualitative image quality (encompassing both overall image quality and RAV visualization quality) using a 5-point Likert scale.

43062466.label: Results
43062466.text: Quantitative evaluation showed that VMI energy level and reconstruction kernel were associated with changes in quantitative image quality metrics, with significant interactions between energy level and reconstruction kernel for all four quantitative metrics (all P < 0.001). Exploratory analyses suggested BMI-related interactions in RAV attenuation and subjective visualization quality. Lower keV increased RAV CT attenuation and CNR, with the highest values at 40 keV across all BMI groups. Qualitative evaluation demonstrated a 100% RAV visualization rate across all reconstruction settings and BMI groups, with median visualization scores ranging from 3.0 to 5.0. Inter-reader agreement was excellent (weighted κ = 0.82).

43062466.label: Conclusion
43062466.text: PCCT provides favorable RAV visualization across the investigated BMI groups, with low-keV imaging and smoother reconstruction kernels associated with improved visualization quality.

43076966.label: Objective
43076966.text: Automated identification and extraction of recommendations for additional imaging (RAI) from radiology reports could facilitate closed-loop tracking and follow-up completion. We compare a prompt-engineered GPT-4.1 large language model (LLM) versus a validated encoder-only transformer deep learning model (bidirectional encoder representations from transformers [BERT]) for detection of RAI in abdominopelvic computed tomography (CTAP) reports, and evaluate GPT-4.1 for extraction of actionable RAI elements.

43076966.label: Methods
43076966.text: This retrospective study included CTAP reports from a multi-institution system in 2023. LLM and BERT were used to identify RAI from radiology reports; LLM also extracted RAI actionable elements (modality, body part, time frame, rationale). Recall, precision, F1, and accuracy for RAI detection were determined using human-annotated reference standard. Paired comparison between each model's accuracy used McNemar's test. LLM recall, precision, F1, and accuracy for actionable element extraction were computed. Element prevalence was compared using chi-square test.

43076966.label: Results
43076966.text: 2000 random reports for unique patients (58% women; mean age 58.5 ± 17.5) included 215 RAI within 206 reports. For RAI detection, GPT-4.1 recall, precision, F1 and accuracy were 95.6%, 98.5%, 97.0% and 99.4%, respectively; BERT recall, precision, F1 and accuracy were 93.7%, 96.5%, 95.1% and 99.0% (p = 0.16). Recommendation element recall were as follows: 100.0% for time frame, 93.9% for body part, 90.2% for rationale, and 94.2% for modality. Precision were 100.0%, 95.7%, 94.6% and 86.1%, respectively. 29/215 (13.5%) RAI were complete (specified all actionable elements). Prevalence of actionable elements varied (p < 0.001), highest for rationale (215/215, 100%), followed by body part (213/215, 99.1%), modality (191/215, 88.8%), and time frame (31/215, 14.4%).

43076966.label: Conclusion
43076966.text: GPT-4.1 demonstrated high accuracy for extraction of RAI and enabled accurate extraction of actionable elements. LLM integration into radiology workflows can facilitate automatic closed-loop communication and tracking of recommended imaging, which may reduce diagnostic delays.
